nameStory: Cypress vine gets its name from its delicate, feathery leaves that look remarkably like the foliage of cypress trees. The 'vine' part is obvious - this climbing beauty can scramble up to 20 feet in a single growing season! It's also called 'hummingbird vine' because those tiny ruby-red flowers are perfectly shaped for hummingbird beaks.
description: Cypress vine is a fast-growing annual climbing vine with incredibly delicate, lacy foliage that looks almost fern-like. The leaves are cut into thread-thin segments, giving the whole plant an airy, feathery appearance. Small, bright red trumpet-shaped flowers dot the vine throughout summer, and the whole plant can climb 10-20 feet in a single season using twining stems.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are cut into extremely thin, thread-like segments that feel soft and delicate to the touch, creating a feathery, almost fern-like appearance completely unlike other morning glories

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small bright red trumpet-shaped flowers about 1 inch long with a white throat, opening in morning and closing by afternoon like other morning glories

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Twining vine that spirals counterclockwise around supports, climbing rapidly up fences, trellises, or other plants

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, green, flexible stems that feel tender and break easily when bent, with a slightly sticky sap

habitat: In New England, cypress vine is occasionally found in gardens as an ornamental, sometimes escaping to grow wild in disturbed areas, fence rows, and field edges. It prefers full sun and well-drained soil, and being tropical in origin, it's quite rare this far north and only survives as an annual.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate late in spring when soil warms up, producing the first feathery leaves in late May or June.
seasonality.summer: Rapid growth and flowering period from July through September, with bright red flowers opening each morning. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming until first frost kills the entire plant. Small round seed capsules may form if flowers are pollinated.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts survive - this tropical vine is completely killed by New England's first hard frost.

funFact: Each tiny red flower opens for just one day, unfurling in the morning like a miniature trumpet and closing forever by afternoon - but the plant produces so many flowers that there are always fresh ones opening each day throughout the summer!
confusionNotes: The thread-like, feathery leaves make cypress vine impossible to confuse with other morning glories, which all have broad, heart-shaped or lobed leaves. If you see red trumpet flowers on a vine with lacy, fern-like foliage, you've found cypress vine.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'cypress vine,' this plant is not related to cypress trees at all - it's actually a morning glory! The name comes purely from the visual similarity of the feathery foliage. It's also sometimes called 'star glory' because the flowers have five pointed petals that form a star shape.
compareHints: Cypress vine is instantly distinguished from all other morning glories by its incredibly fine, thread-like leaf segments - every other morning glory in New England has broad, solid leaves. Red morning glory has similar red flowers but typical heart-shaped morning glory leaves, while common morning glory has purple flowers and broad heart-shaped leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common morning-glory has the largest flowers among New England's morning-glories, with those distinctive heart-shaped leaves that lack the three-lobed structure of ivy-leaved morning-glory.

Among New England morning-glories, ivy-leaved is distinguished by its three-lobed leaves - common morning-glory has unlobed heart-shaped leaves, while white morning-glory has much smaller flowers and often heart-shaped but sometimes three-lobed leaves.

Garden Morning Glory stands out from its Ipomoea cousins with its large flower size and vibrant blue color range - Common Morning Glory has smaller, more purple-pink flowers, while Ivy-leaved Morning Glory has distinctly lobed leaves rather than the simple heart shape.

Among its morning glory relatives, moonflower stands out for its exclusively nighttime blooming and pure white color - most other Ipomoea species bloom during the day in shades of purple, blue, pink, or red.
Unlike its morning glory relatives that are primarily grown for their showy trumpet flowers, sweet potato is grown for foliage and edible tubers, rarely flowering in New England's climate.
Red morning glory stands out from other New England morning glories primarily by its small size and brilliant red color - most others have much larger purple, blue, or white flowers.
Among New England morning-glories, wild potato vine stands out with its pure white flowers that have pink throats, while most others have purple, blue, or pink flowers.

Among New England morning glories, scarlet creeper is the only one with consistently bright red flowers - common morning glory has purple flowers, ivy-leaved morning glory has blue to purple blooms, and moonflower has large white flowers.

White morning-glory stands out from its Ipomoea relatives by having the smallest flowers in the genus - much tinier than the dinner-plate-sized blooms of moonflower or the vibrant purple trumpets of common morning-glory.
